2.1: SLE is a serious, chronic autoimmune disease that affects multiple organ systems and follows an unpredictable, relapsing course. Despite the available treatments, a substantial proportion of patients do not achieve adequate disease control or experience recurrent flares. The reliance on broad-acting immunosuppressants and the cumulative toxicity of long-term glucocorticoid use underscore a clear unmet need for new, targeted and better-tolerated therapies. This trial is a Phase 2 proof-of-concept trial of the investigational product in patients with SLE and active cutaneous manifestations.
4.2.1: The primary estimand was defined in alignment with the addendum to ICH E9 (R1) to provide a reliable and clinically interpretable estimate of the treatment effect in adult patients with active disease. Change from baseline in the primary score was selected as the primary endpoint because it is the most widely validated and regulatory-accepted instrument for quantifying disease activity.
4.2.2: This is a parallel-group randomized placebo-controlled trial. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the investigational product or placebo. Allowing re-treatment will more closely mimic how these drugs are given in clinical practice (see Section 6.2 for the rationale for the dose and regimen selection). A 2:1 randomization ratio was chosen to broaden the safety experience with the investigational product with a minimal reduction in study power.
4.2.3: A placebo control was chosen to minimize any potential bias that knowledge of the assigned treatment might introduce in the participant's self-reported outcomes and the physician's assessments. The placebo will consist of the diluent alone, will be visually indistinguishable from the prepared investigational product and will have the same pH. Blinded and unblinded trial personnel at each trial site will be identified and trained in maintenance of the blind.
4.2.4: Patients hospitalized for the condition are at increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes including rehospitalization and death in the first months following discharge. Earlier phase 2 trials suggest effects on clinical outcomes at 30 days, when all participants were followed through 30 days after a single infusion. Thus, this trial is designed to allow confirmation of the benefit on 30-day outcomes.
